quotations.summary: After forty days of fasting, Satan commands Christ to turn stones to bread. Christ's reply — that man lives by every word of God, not bread alone — turns a physical temptation into a declaration about what truly sustains life.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.
quotations.church_scripture_text_ot: And he humbled thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna, which thou knewest not, neither did thy fathers know; that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live.
study_questions: Deuteronomy 8:3 addresses Israel after forty years in the wilderness — the same setting Christ is now in. The manna was given to teach dependence on God's word, not on physical provision alone. Christ cites the lesson Israel was supposed to have learned.

Christ does not defend himself with personal authority or a miracle. He answers every temptation in the wilderness with Deuteronomy — the book of covenant renewal given to Israel on the edge of the promised land. This is Deuteronomy exclusively as a source in the wilderness.
The principle being pressed: spiritual life is sustained by God's word, not by comfort or provision. Satan's offer was real bread; Christ's answer is that real life is not about bread.
quotations.notes: Verified against churchofjesuschrist.org. Direct quotation with explicit citation formula 'it is written'.

quotations.summary: When Satan quotes scripture to invite Christ to prove God's protection by jumping from the temple pinnacle, Christ refuses with another Deuteronomy verse: you do not test God by engineering situations that require rescue.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.
quotations.church_scripture_text_ot: Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as ye tempted him in Massah.
study_questions: Massah was the place where Israel demanded water and accused God of abandoning them — an act of faithless testing. Christ's refusal to jump is a refusal to repeat that pattern. Genuine faith does not require God to perform on demand.

Satan's second temptation used scripture (Ps 91:11–12) to construct a false argument. Christ counters not with raw authority but with a more governing principle from Deuteronomy. Deuteronomy outranks the Psalms as the covenant foundation.
The second wilderness temptation, still answered with Deuteronomy. The pattern holds: Satan, Deuteronomy, correction.

quotations.summary: Satan offers all the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship. Christ dismisses him with Deuteronomy's foundational covenant command: God alone is to be worshiped and served.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.
quotations.church_scripture_text_ot: Thou shalt fear the LORD thy God, and serve him, and shalt swear by his name.
study_questions: This is the only moment in the temptation narrative where Christ commands Satan directly — 'Get thee hence' — before citing scripture. The Deuteronomy verse is the ground for the dismissal, not a negotiating tactic.

All three wilderness temptations were answered exclusively with Deuteronomy. This is the only book Christ cites against Satan, and Deuteronomy 6 is the core covenant chapter — the Shema chapter, containing Israel's foundational confession of God's oneness and exclusivity.
The principle: undivided loyalty to God is not one virtue among many — it is the first and governing principle. Worship of anything else is a category error, not a preference question.
quotations.notes: Verified against churchofjesuschrist.org. Third and final wilderness temptation.

quotations.summary: The sixth and final Sermon antithesis: you have heard it said to love your neighbor — but Christ extends Lev 19:18 to enemies as well. This is the highest reach of the higher law, pressing the command beyond its natural boundary.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: Ye have heard that it hath been said, Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy. But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;
quotations.church_scripture_text_ot: Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.
study_questions: Leviticus 19:18 commanded love of neighbor within Israel. The addition 'and hate thine enemy' is not in the biblical text — it is an interpretive tradition that had narrowed the command's scope. Christ does not abolish Lev 19:18; he restores and expands it.

The extension to enemies is the moment the command becomes hardest. Loving a neighbor is natural; loving an enemy requires a transformation of will. This is the direction Christ consistently presses with this verse across all four occasions.
This is the first of four distinct occasions where Christ cites Lev 19:18 — the most-cited OT passage in this catalog. Each occasion extends or deepens the same core principle.
quotations.notes: Verified against churchofjesuschrist.org. First of four Lev 19:18 occasions.

quotations.summary: The first antithesis of the Sermon on the Mount: you have heard it said, do not murder — but Christ extends the principle inward, to anger and contempt. The law set a floor; Christ raises the ceiling.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill; and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment: But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment.
study_questions: The Mosaic prohibition on murder is the legal minimum. Christ does not abolish it — he shows that it addressed behavior, not the internal state that produces the behavior. Anger and contempt carry the same moral weight as the act they lead toward.

The Sermon's antitheses all follow the same pattern: 'You have heard… but I say unto you.' Christ speaks here with authority equal to or greater than the law's original source. He is not commenting on the law from outside it.
The Sermon draws exclusively from the Pentateuch — Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy. No prophetic books appear in the Sermon antitheses. The audience is Jewish; the law is the shared ground.
quotations.notes: Verified against churchofjesuschrist.org. First of six Sermon antitheses.

quotations.summary: A young man asks what good thing he must do to have eternal life. Christ lists several commandments from Exodus, then closes with 'Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.' The man's claim to have kept them all sets up the harder ask that follows: sell everything and follow him.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: He saith unto him, Which? Jesus said, Thou shalt do no murder, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness, Honour thy father and thy mother: and, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
quotations.church_scripture_text_ot: Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.
study_questions: Christ closes the list of commandments with Lev 19:18, not with one of the ten from Exodus. The placement is deliberate — love of neighbor is the capstone, the command that summarizes the relational half of the law.

The young man says he has kept all these things. Christ does not dispute that claim. Instead, he shows that keeping the commandments is not the ceiling but the floor — the real ask is discipleship, which requires full surrender of security.
Fourth of four Lev 19:18 occasions. Here it appears in a private teaching context rather than a hostile dispute or sermon, and it is used as a benchmark rather than a rebuke.
quotations.notes: Verified against churchofjesuschrist.org. Fourth of four Lev 19:18 occasions.

quotations.summary: The Pharisees question why Christ dines with tax collectors and sinners. He tells them to go and learn what Hosea means — God desires mercy, not sacrifice — because he came for the sick, not the healthy.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
quotations.church_scripture_text_ot: For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
study_questions: Hosea 6:6 comes from a passage where God accuses Israel of a covenant that is 'as a morning cloud' — it looks right but has no depth. The sacrifice-without-mercy pattern is an old problem, not a new Pharisee invention.

Christ's 'go and learn' is a studied rebuke — it implies the Pharisees are teachers of the law who have not yet understood one of its central passages. The instruction to learn is addressed to those who consider themselves experts.
This is the first of two times Christ cites Hosea 6:6 in Matthew. Both occasions are disputes with the Pharisees about what the law actually requires.
quotations.notes: Verified against churchofjesuschrist.org. First of two Hosea 6:6 citations in Matthew.

quotations.summary: The Pharisees accuse Christ's disciples of breaking the Sabbath by plucking grain. Christ cites Hosea 6:6 again — this time with a sharper edge: 'If ye had known what this meaneth.' The same verse, the same accusers, but the indictment is now deeper.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: But if ye had known what this meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice, ye would not have condemned the guiltless.
quotations.church_scripture_text_ot: For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
study_questions: The shift from 'go and learn' (Matt 9:13) to 'if ye had known' (Matt 12:7) is notable. The Pharisees have presumably encountered this teaching before. The second citation implies they were given the chance to learn and did not.

Matthew 12 continues with more Sabbath conflict and ends with the Pharisees beginning to plot against Christ. The citation of Hosea at the beginning of this sequence frames the entire confrontation: they are condemning the guiltless because they have not understood what mercy requires.
Hosea 6:6 appears only in Matthew across the Gospel record. Its use is specific to the conflict with the Pharisees. No other Gospel cites it.
quotations.notes: Verified against churchofjesuschrist.org. Second Hosea 6:6 citation, slightly escalated rhetorical framing.

quotations.summary: A lawyer asks which commandment is greatest. Christ answers with two: love God (Deuteronomy 6:5) and love your neighbor (Leviticus 19:18). On these two, he says, hang all the law and the prophets.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
quotations.church_scripture_text_ot: And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might.
study_questions: The lawyer's question was a trap — Jewish scholars debated which commandment was greatest, and any answer could be used against Christ. Instead of ranking among 613 commandments, Christ names the two that organize all the others.

Both laws come from the Torah: Deuteronomy 6:5 (the Shema chapter) and Leviticus 19:18. The pairing is not original to Christ — rabbinic tradition connected them — but his statement that 'on these two hang all the law and the prophets' gives the synthesis authoritative finality.

Leviticus 19:18 is the P1 passage — the most-cited OT text in this catalog. Its appearance here alongside the Shema shows it was not a peripheral law but one Christ considered structurally central to the entire covenant.
quotations.notes: Verified against churchofjesuschrist.org. Contains both Deut 6:5 and Lev 19:18. One of four distinct Lev 19:18 occasions.

quotations.summary: Christ poses a riddle to the Pharisees: if David calls the Messiah 'my Lord' in Psalm 110, how can the Messiah merely be David's son? The question implies the Messiah is David's superior — pointing to divine identity, not just Davidic lineage.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: He saith unto them, How then doth David in spirit call him Lord, saying, The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand, till I make thine enemies thy footstool?
quotations.church_scripture_text_ot: The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.
study_questions: Psalm 110 was understood as messianic in first-century Judaism. Christ uses it not to identify himself directly but to pose the logical problem: if the Messiah is purely David's descendant, why does David call him Lord? The argument by question silences his opponents.

This is self-identification by implication: Christ is inviting his hearers to follow the logic to its conclusion without saying it outright. The Pharisees cannot answer because answering honestly would require them to acknowledge who he is.
Psalm 110:1 appears again at the trial (Matt 26:64), where Christ cites it directly to affirm his divine identity. The riddle here and the declaration there are bookends.

quotations.summary: Christ ends his Passion-week denunciation of Jerusalem with a lament: your house is left desolate, and you will not see me again until you say 'Blessed is he that cometh.' The Hallel psalm of joyful entry becomes a grief-soaked threshold — a conditional return that has not yet happened.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: For I say unto you, Ye shall not see me henceforth, till ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.
quotations.church_scripture_text_ot: Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the LORD: we have blessed you out of the house of the LORD.
study_questions: Psalm 118 was sung at Passover and used in the triumphal entry days earlier. The crowds quoted it in joy; Christ now quotes it in grief. The same psalm, one week apart, from celebration to desolation.

The passive construction — 'you will not see me until you say' — is the form of lament that leaves the door open. Christ is not pronouncing permanent abandonment. The return is promised; the condition is unmet.

Ps 118:26 appears twice in Christ's ministry, both times in grief contexts: once in the Lukan lament over Jerusalem during his earlier ministry (Luke 13:35) and here in the Passion-week denunciation. The dominant mode across both occasions is lament, not triumph.
quotations.notes: Verified against churchofjesuschrist.org. Second of two Ps 118:26 citations, Passion week setting.

quotations.summary: The high priest asks under oath: are you the Messiah, the Son of God? Christ answers 'Thou hast said' — an affirmation — then immediately cites both Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13 to describe what they will yet see. The two OT passages together make the fullest claim of identity in the Gospels.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: Jesus saith unto him, Thou hast said: nevertheless I say unto you, Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven.
quotations.church_scripture_text_ot: The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool. / I saw in the night visions, and, behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
study_questions: The composite citation — Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13 together — is the most concentrated claim of divine identity in the trial. Psalm 110:1 places him at God's right hand; Daniel 7:13 shows him coming in universal dominion. Together they describe the arc from present exaltation to future return.
The high priest tears his robes immediately after hearing this — the signal of blasphemy under Jewish law. The citation is understood as a claim to divine status, not merely messianic kingship.

Daniel 7:13 does not appear until this moment — Christ cites Daniel only in private settings or at his trial, never in public teaching. Its use here, at the precise moment the legal process reaches its climax, is the first and only public invocation of this passage.
quotations.notes: Verified against churchofjesuschrist.org. Composite citation. Both RP-007 (Ps 110:1) and RP-008 (Dan 7:13) reference this entry.

quotations.summary: From the cross, in his own language — Aramaic — Christ cries the opening words of Psalm 22: 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' The only moment in the Gospels where Christ prays in Aramaic rather than citing scripture in Greek or Hebrew, addressed to the Father alone.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
quotations.church_scripture_text_ot: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?
study_questions: Psalm 22 begins in desolation but ends in vindication and universal praise. Whether Christ intends to invoke the full psalm or whether this is purely the cry of the moment is a studied question. What is clear: he is voicing something true — the felt distance of divine presence at the height of the Atonement.

All the cross citations are from the Psalms. The Psalms are personal poetry addressed to God — the voice of suffering, trust, and praise. At the cross, Christ draws only from this register. The cross is not a moment for law or prophecy; it is a moment for the language of lament.

The Aramaic is unusual — every other scripture citation in the Gospels is reported in Greek. The retention of the Aramaic suggests this is as close as any Gospel text comes to recording Christ's exact words.
quotations.notes: Verified against churchofjesuschrist.org. Aramaic preserved in Greek text.

quotations.summary: In the Nephite Sermon at Bountiful, Christ delivers the same antithesis he gave in Galilee: love your neighbor — and now love your enemies. To the Nephites he adds 'that ye may be the children of your Father who is in heaven.' The higher law is framed in terms of becoming, not just behaving.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: But I say unto you, love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them who despitefully use you and persecute you;
quotations.church_scripture_text_ot: Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.
study_questions: The 3 Nephi Sermon is distinct from the Galilean Sermon — different audience, different time, Christ in his resurrected state dictating what is to be written. The antithesis reappears, but the framing is slightly different: the reason to love enemies is to become like your Father in heaven.

Leviticus 19:18 is the P1 passage — Christ cites it on four distinct occasions, more than any other OT text. In 3 Nephi he extends it beyond neighbors to enemies, as he did in Galilee. The extension is consistent across both audiences separated by decades and an ocean.

In me are fulfilled,' Christ tells the Nephites, referring to the law of Moses broadly. The higher law he presses toward is not the abolition of Lev 19:18 but its extension — love applied to those outside your community.
quotations.notes: Verified against churchofjesuschrist.org. Third of four distinct Lev 19:18 occasions.

quotations.summary: Christ commands the Nephites to stand and recites Isaiah 52:1-2 — the call to Zion to awake, shake off the dust, and put on her beautiful garments. He then explains that he is fulfilling this scripture in their midst.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: And then shall the words come to pass that are written: Awake, awake again, and put on thy strength, O Zion; put on thy beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city, for henceforth there shall no more come into thee the uncircumcised and the unclean.
quotations.church_scripture_text_ot: Awake, awake; put on thy strength, O Zion; put on thy beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city: for henceforth there shall no more come into thee the uncircumcised and the unclean.
study_questions: Isaiah dominates 3 Nephi. Of the 14 distinct Isaiah citation occasions in the full catalog, the majority occur in the Nephite discourse. Christ devotes significant time to reading, interpreting, and applying Isaiah — more so than any other OT book in any other setting.

The gathering-of-Israel frame governs the entire 3 Nephi Isaiah section. Isaiah 52's command to Zion to awaken is presented as a now-being-fulfilled reality. Christ is not predicting future gathering; he is announcing it.

The Brass Plates version of Isaiah may differ slightly from KJV wording. The 3 Nephi text is slightly different in places. These differences are worth noting but do not change the core identification of the OT source.
quotations.notes: Verified against churchofjesuschrist.org. Part of the extended Isaiah reading in 3 Nephi 20-22.

quotations.summary: In a latter-day revelation, Christ describes the future moment when the Jews will recognize him — they will ask about the wounds in his hands, and he will answer them directly. This is the only entry in the full catalog where Christ identifies himself as the wounded figure of a specific OT prophecy, in the presence of the people the prophecy was written for.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: And then shall the Jews look upon me and say: What are these wounds in thine hands and in thy feet? Then shall they know that I am the Lord; for I will say unto them: These wounds are the wounds with which I was wounded in the house of my friends. I am he who was lifted up. I am Jesus that was crucified. I am the Son of God.
quotations.church_scripture_text_ot: And one shall say unto him, What are these wounds in thine hands? Then he shall answer, Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends.
study_questions: Zechariah 13 is a chapter about a shepherd who is struck — 'Smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered' (Zech 13:7) is the verse Christ himself cites at Gethsemane. Zechariah 13:6 is the recognition question from that same prophetic context.

This scene appears nowhere in the Gospels or 3 Nephi. D&C 45 preserves it as a future event — the moment of Jewish recognition at Christ's return. It is the only entry in the catalog where Christ directly connects a wound prophecy to himself in a recognition context.

The self-identification is explicit and multi-layered: 'I am the Lord,' 'I am Jesus that was crucified,' 'I am the Son of God.' No other catalog entry contains this density of first-person identity declaration.
quotations.notes: Verified against D&C 45 on churchofjesuschrist.org. One of three D&C-unique contributions to the full catalog.

quotations.summary: In a latter-day revelation about his Second Coming, Christ quotes Isaiah 63's wine-press passage in first person — 'I have trodden the wine-press alone' — claiming the image of atoning suffering and Second Coming judgment as his own experience. This is the only place in the full 108-entry catalog where Christ speaks in his own voice about the cost of the Atonement using Old Testament language.
quotations.church_scripture_text_nt: And now the year of my redeemed is come; and they shall mention the loving kindness of their Lord, and all that he has bestowed upon them according to his goodness, and according to his loving kindness, forever and ever. In all their afflictions he was afflicted. And the angel of his presence saved them; and in his love, and in his pity, he redeemed them, and bore them, and carried them all the days of old; Yea, and Enoch also, and they who were with him; the prophets who were before him; and Noah also, and they who were before him; and Moses also, and they who were before him; And from Moses to Elijah, and from Elijah to John, who were with Christ in his resurrection, and the holy apostles, with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, shall be in the presence of the Lamb. And the graves of the saints shall be opened; and they shall come forth and stand on the right hand of the Lamb, when he shall stand upon Mount Zion, and upon the holy city, the New Jerusalem; and they shall sing the song of the Lamb, day and night forever and ever. And for this cause, that men might be made partakers of the glories which were to be revealed, the Lord sent forth the fulness of his gospel, his everlasting covenant, reasoning in plainness and simplicity— To prepare the weak for those things which are coming on the earth, and for the Lord's errand in the day when the weak shall confound the wise, and the little one become a strong nation, and two shall put their tens of thousands to flight. And by the weak things of the earth the Lord shall thrash the nations by the power of his Spirit. And for this cause these commandments were given; they were commanded to be kept from the world in the day that they were given, but now are to go forth unto all flesh— And this according to the mind and will of the Lord, who ruleth over all flesh. And unto him that repenteth and sanctifieth himself before the Lord shall be given eternal life. And upon them that hearken not to the voice of the Lord shall be fulfilled that which was written by the prophet Moses, that they should be cut off from among the people. And also that which was written by the prophet Malachi: For, behold, the day cometh that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble; and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the Lord of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch. Hearken and hear, O ye my people, saith your God; and your God I am, even Jesus Christ. Wherefore, labor ye, labor ye in my vineyard for the last time—for the last time call upon the inhabitants of the earth. For in mine own due time will I come upon the earth in judgment, and my people shall be redeemed and shall reign with me on earth. For the great Millennium, of which I have spoken by the mouth of my servants, shall come. For Satan shall be bound, and when he is loosed again he shall only reign for a little season, and then cometh the end of the earth. And he that liveth in righteousness shall be changed in the twinkling of an eye, and the earth shall pass away so as by fire. And the wicked shall go away into unquenchable fire, and their end no man knoweth on earth, nor ever shall know, until they come before me in judgment. Hearken ye to these things even as I have spoken them unto you. Go ye hence, and seal up these things, saith the Lord God, for I will reveal myself from heaven with power and great glory, with all the hosts thereof, and dwell in righteousness with men on earth a thousand years, and the wicked shall not stand. And again, verily, verily, I say unto you, and it hath gone forth in a firm decree, by the will of the Father, that mine apostles, the Twelve which were with me in my ministry at Jerusalem, shall stand at my right hand at the day of my coming in a pillar of fire, being clothed with robes of righteousness, with crowns upon their heads, in glory even as I am, to judge the whole house of Israel, even as many as have loved me and kept my commandments, and none else. For a trump shall sound both long and loud, even as upon Mount Sinai, and all the earth shall quake, and they shall come forth—yea, even the dead which died in me, to receive a crown of righteousness, and to be clothed upon, even as I am, to be with me, that we may be one.
quotations.church_scripture_text_ot: Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? this that is glorious in his apparel, travelling in the greatness of his strength? I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save. Wherefore art thou red in thine apparel, and thy garments like him that treadeth in the winefat? I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me: for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury; and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments, and I will stain all my raiment.
study_questions: Isaiah 63 was written centuries before Christ's birth. In D&C 133, Christ claims it as his own experience — 'I have trodden the wine-press alone.' This is distinct from citing Isaiah as prophecy or instruction; it is claiming Isaiah's imagery as personal testimony.

The wine-press image describes both the Atonement (atoning suffering accomplished alone) and the Second Coming (judgment of the wicked). Christ applies both dimensions to himself — it is simultaneously a statement about what he has already done and what he will yet do.

This entry is one of three D&C-unique contributions to the catalog: content that appears in Christ's words in D&C but not in the Gospels or 3 Nephi. The other two are the wounds-in-the-hands recognition scene (DC-009) and the naming of Ezekiel explicitly in a citation formula (DC-004).
quotations.notes: Verified against D&C 133 on churchofjesuschrist.org. One of three D&C-unique contributions. DC-016 covers Isa 63:3 specifically.

audience_settings.label: Wilderness — Temptations
audience_settings.description: The forty-day fast and three temptations by Satan.

audience_settings.label: Sermon on the Mount
audience_settings.description: The Galilean sermon to the multitude and disciples.

audience_settings.label: Public teaching
audience_settings.description: Synagogue teaching, crowds, general public discourse.

audience_settings.label: Hostile questioners
audience_settings.description: Pharisees, scribes, and lawyers challenging Christ.

audience_settings.label: Private disciples
audience_settings.description: Teaching given privately to the Twelve or a small group.

audience_settings.label: Last Supper
audience_settings.description: The final evening with the Twelve before the arrest.

audience_settings.label: Passion week
audience_settings.description: The days between the triumphal entry and the arrest.

audience_settings.label: Nephite gathering at Bountiful
audience_settings.description: Christ's ministry to the Nephites after his resurrection, recorded in 3 Nephi.

audience_settings.label: Doctrine and Covenants
audience_settings.description: Latter-day revelation given through the Prophet Joseph Smith and early Church leaders.

repeated_passage_groups.observation: The most-cited OT passage in Christ's ministry. Appears in four distinct settings — Galilean Sermon, Great Commandment, Nephite Sermon, and the Rich Young Ruler — always pushing toward the same principle: love your neighbor is not a peripheral command but a structurally central one.
Cited twice in Matthew against the Pharisees. The first time: 'go and learn what it means.' The second: 'if you had known what it means.' Both are disputes about what the law actually requires.
open_questions: QO-1: Does the shift in phrasing represent deliberate escalation?

repeated_passage_groups.observation: Cited as a riddle to the Pharisees (Matt 22:44) and then at the trial as a direct affirmation (Matt 26:64). The question form and the declaration form together show Christ pointing toward the same identity claim from opposite directions.
Christ cites Daniel 7:13 only in private or trial settings — never in public teaching. At the trial it is paired with Ps 110:1 to form the most concentrated identity claim in the Gospels.
The Hallel psalm of triumphal entry is cited by Christ in grief contexts, not joy. Both occasions are laments over Jerusalem's unreadiness to receive him.

patterns.name: Wilderness — Deuteronomy exclusively
patterns.description: Every temptation by Satan in the wilderness is answered with Deuteronomy. No other OT book appears in this setting. Deuteronomy 6 and 8 are from the covenant-renewal discourses given to Israel on the edge of the promised land — the same threshold setting Christ is in.

patterns.name: Hostile questioners — meeting them in their own texts
patterns.description: When challenged by Pharisees and lawyers, Christ consistently cites texts from the Torah and Psalms that his opponents should already know and accept. He does not introduce unfamiliar material; he shows they have not understood what is already in front of them.

patterns.name: Sermon on the Mount — Pentateuch only
patterns.description: All six Sermon antitheses cite from the Pentateuch (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy). No prophetic books appear. The Sermon is addressed to a Jewish audience; the Pentateuch is the shared covenant foundation.

patterns.name: Private disciples and the trial — Daniel only
patterns.description: Daniel 7:13 appears only in private settings with the disciples (Olivet Discourse) or at the trial. It is never cited in public teaching or against opponents. Its use is reserved for contexts requiring the most explicit identity claim.

patterns.name: Passion arc — shift to Psalms
patterns.description: As the Passion week progresses, the OT citations shift from law and prophecy to Psalms. The cross citations are exclusively from Psalms. This mirrors the Psalms' function as personal lament and prayer — the voice of suffering directed to God.

patterns.name: Nephite discourse — Isaiah saturation
patterns.description: Isaiah dominates the 3 Nephi record. Christ devotes significant teaching time to reading and interpreting Isaiah — more than any other OT book in any other setting. The gathering-of-Israel frame governs the entire section.

patterns.name: Hosea as Pharisee-specific diagnostic
patterns.description: Hosea 6:6 appears only in Matthew, only in disputes with the Pharisees. It is not cited in any other Gospel or setting. Its specific application to the mercy-vs-sacrifice argument is targeted.

patterns.name: Cross citations — Psalms only, addressed to the Father
patterns.description: The only citations from the cross are from the Psalms. They are not addressed to bystanders but to God — the language of Lament Psalms, which model honest suffering and trust before God.

patterns.name: Three citation modes
patterns.description: Across the catalog, Christ's OT citations cluster into three dominant modes: corrective teaching (reframing or fulfilling misunderstood law), self-identification (using scripture as a lens for his own identity and mission), and lament (voicing grief and suffering through Psalm language).
